title: Cutter Flank-Wear Estimation Between Inspections Using Measured Wear Changes and Sensor Signals
content: Flank wear is measured only at periodic inspections because measurement interrupts machining, leaving the wear of intermediate cuts unknown. Existing methods fill these gaps with assumed wear values before training, and whether their per-cut estimates match actual wear is rarely tested. This study asks whether wear changes measured between inspections suffice to train a per-cut wear estimator, and when sensor signals add value. A gated recurrent unit predicts each cut's wear increase from sensor signals and is trained only on the measured change over each inspection interval. In 28 hard-turning runs measured after every cut, five-cut inspections were simulated and withheld measurements used for scoring. For cutting conditions excluded from training, estimates made during machining had a root mean square error of 4.4 µm, about 3% of final wear, against 6.1 µm without sensors and 4.6–4.8 µm when trained on assumed wear values. The estimates followed the wear-rate trend, not cut-to-cut variation. A post hoc analysis suggested that sensors helped most in the first inspection interval of a new tool under an unseen condition, before its wear rate was measured; afterwards, rate extrapolation was as accurate. Measured-interval supervision is feasible, and the value of sensors depends on the inspection history.
